data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without smuggling in induction by redefining rational action as the strategic selection of the most testable (and thus most falsifiable) hypothesis, rather than the most probable one; this accepts the cost that 'rationality' no longer guarantees proximity to truth or practical success, but only maximizes the speed of error elimination.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one assumes that the ultimate goal of science is immediate practical reliability rather than long-term truth approximation, the preference becomes indefensible without induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' is interpreted as a belief in higher probability rather than a decision rule for testing, the argument collapses into the very induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the uniformity of nature is required to justify even the strategy of error elimination, then the non-inductive claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven) and the methodological rule of preference (which aims at high informational content). It posits that preferring a severely tested theory is rational because it has survived attempts to destroy it, leaving it as the best available target for future falsification, whereas an untested or weakly corroborated theory might hide errors. This avoids induction by refusing to infer future success from past survival, instead treating past survival as a prerequisite for being a worthy opponent in the next round of testing.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
